analysis.one_liner: Exempts federal construction contracts under $100,000 from paying locally prevailing wages.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have removed prevailing-wage requirements from most federal construction contracts, never received a committee vote and died when the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Davis-Bacon Act requires contractors on federally financed construction to pay the locally prevailing wage — in many areas, union-scale pay. This bill would have raised the contract size that triggers that rule from $2,000 to $100,000, exempting the large majority of federal construction contracts. Supporters framed it as updating a 1931 threshold that no longer fit modern contract sizes and reducing compliance costs; the effect would have been that most federally funded construction jobs no longer had to pay prevailing wages.
analysis.who_benefits: Construction contractors doing federal work, especially smaller contracts under $100,000, would gain: with no prevailing-wage obligation, they could pay less than union-scale wages, cut labor costs, and submit lower bids without the paperwork of wage determinations and certified payrolls. Taxpayers would see some savings on federal projects through lower bids.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the Davis-Bacon coverage threshold from $2,000 to $100,000, so only the largest federally financed construction contracts would be required to pay locally prevailing wages [S2][S3].
The Davis-Bacon Act applies prevailing-wage requirements to laborers and mechanics on federally financed or assisted construction of public buildings and works [S2].
Contractors freed of the requirement could pay below prevailing rates and avoid the administrative costs of wage determinations and payroll certifications on most contracts [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers — laborers and mechanics — on federally funded projects under $100,000 would bear the cost: their wages would no longer be pegged to local prevailing rates, and in many areas those rates reflect union scale. Unionized contractors who follow prevailing-wage standards would compete against bids built on lower pay. Workers lose wage protection; taxpayers gain a portion of it back in lower project costs.

drawbacks.text: Raising the threshold to $100,000 would exempt most federally financed construction contracts from prevailing-wage coverage, so workers on those jobs could legally be paid less than the local prevailing rate [S2][S3].

The Davis-Bacon prevailing-wage floor is a wage standard for construction workers on public projects; weakening it on most contracts lowers pay for the workers those rules were written to protect [S2].

Supporters' core argument — that the $2,000 trigger set in 1931 was badly outdated and its compliance costs inflate federal project costs — has force, but the bill addressed it by lifting wage protection rather than indexing the threshold to inflation, which would have updated the number without removing coverage from most contracts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real but modest taxpayer savings on federal construction through lower bids and less paperwork. The cost fell on a specific group of workers — laborers and mechanics on federal projects — who would lose the wage floor on nearly every contract they work. Weighing contractor and taxpayer savings against construction workers' wages, the design was lopsided: it modernized an outdated number by removing protection rather than adjusting it, and the gain for the general taxpayer was far smaller than the wage loss concentrated on affected workers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, then to its Workforce Protections Subcommittee, and never came up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Cass Ballenger (R-NC), joined by Rep. Howard Coble and three other Republican cosponsors, introduced the bill on June 7, 2001 [S1][S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and the Workforce the day it was introduced [S5].
On August 10, 2001, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, where it remained; it received no markup, no floor vote, and no Senate action [S5].
The Congress ended January 3, 2003, with the bill still in committee [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, federal construction contractors never got the labor-cost savings it would have created, and construction workers on federally funded projects kept prevailing-wage protection. The larger 2000s-era efforts to scale back Davis-Bacon also failed, leaving the wage floor intact for the next Congresses to litigate.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Construction workers kept their wage floor

for.name: Rep. Cass Ballenger
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Davis-Bacon Modernization Act to raise the prevailing-wage contract threshold from $2,000 to $100,000.

for.name: Rep. Howard Coble
for.what_they_did: Joined the introduction of the bill.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and referred it to the Workforce Protections Subcommittee; it never received a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and Davis-Bacon proposals in this era generally split along party lines, with Republicans seeking to scale back the wage mandate and Democrats and building-trades unions defending it; no votes were ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have let contractors on federally funded jobs under $100,000 pay below prevailing wages and skip wage-compliance paperwork, cutting their costs and bids. The savings came out of their workers' paychecks, so the industry's gain was directly the workers' loss.

Prevailing-wage rules anchor union-scale pay across the construction labor market; exempting most federal contracts from them would have undercut the standard union contractors and their workers compete against. The bill died before any of this took effect.
Laborers and mechanics on federally financed jobs would have lost the guarantee of locally prevailing pay on most contracts. The bill never passed, so their pay standard held.
